newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU pressed to agree farm animal transport rules.
newsitem.headline: EU pressed to agree farm animal transport rules.

text.p: Farm animal rest centre rules and route plans for marathon journeys will on Tuesday be submitted for approval to European Union farm ministers, EU diplomats said.

The centres were part of a deal struck in June 1995, after five years of argument, to ease the pain of millions of animals crammed annually into lorries for trips of up to 50 hours from northern producer states to southern slaughter houses.

Swedes and other northerners denounced transport conditions as cruel but southerners, such as Italy, protested that the new rules would raise costs, making imports of live animals uneconomic and throwing tens of thousands of people out of work.

The new rules set a basic eight hours journey limit for cattle, pigs, sheep and other farm animals after which they must be unloaded from their vehicles for 24-hours rest before continuing their journeys.
"They amount to pig hotels," said a Dutch official, adding that the EU's executive Commission has not yet proposed standards for "pig pullmans" transporting the animals.
Germany has criticised delays in agreeing minimum standards for rest centres and vehicles which have prevented implemention of the animal transport rules by the end-1996 deadline.
The Commission says the deadline was unrealistic.

Although officials have settled most of the technical details for the rest centres, including feeding, watering, loading, unloading and animal health requirements, a number of countries still have objections.
Italy has requested EU aid to help equip the centres but the European Commission says the cost should be borne by the industry.
Spain has questioned which veterinary officials should be responsible for running the rest centres and authorising the onward journey of animals.
Sweden wants member states to be allowed to impose higher standards to take account of local climatic conditions.

Britain, backed by Denmark, has requested special treatment for high value breeding pigs. Officials said that the pigs are transported in luxury vehicles and do not need to be unloaded at rest centres, adding it could also put them at risk of disease.
Disagreement over the start-up date for the rest centres still has to be resolved with July 1998 and November 1999 the dates proposed.
Even if farm ministers on Tuesday strike a political deal, the agreement can only be finalised after the European Parliament has given an opinion.
Animal welfare groups, noting the long battle to approve the original transport rules, were cautious about prospects for agreement on rest centres by farm ministers at the first try.
Activists noted strong economic arguments put forward by the transport industry and countries, notably Italy, where the distances would be longest.
"The rules would make transport more expensive and reduce the number of animals being carried," said an official of the Eurogroup for Animal Welfare.
The official criticised the Commission's delay in making proposals for minimum vehicle standards and described the situation as "chaotic."
